title: The Caro-Kann
summary: Solve the bad bishop before you build the wall

steps.title: A Pawn Instead of a Piece
steps.text:
Black met 1.e4 with a c-pawn: a move that attacks nothing, develops nothing and looks like a move thrown away. A move later it pays. Black's ...d5 arrives held up by a pawn rather than by a piece, and the middle of the board gets traded off.

That is how this position happened. Black has one pawn on c6 and an army still at home. White has a pawn on d4 and its first piece out, the knight on e4.

The Caro-Kann is the claim that this is a fine deal for Black.

steps.title: The Bishop Behind the Wall
steps.text:
Most answers to 1.e4 lean on ...e6, and that pawn does two things at once. It holds the center, and it stands in the road of the bishop on c8.

{{e6}}. That bishop has exactly one open diagonal, c8 through h3, and a pawn of its own has just parked on it. What is left is d7, where the bishop blocks the queen and looks at nothing.

Black's c-pawn is already doing the job the e-pawn does elsewhere. So this bishop has no reason to sit and wait for the wall.

steps.prompt: Get that bishop outside the pawns now, onto the square where it also stares at White's knight.
steps.hint: Nothing on the board defends that knight, and the bishop's one open diagonal has exactly one square that attacks it.

steps.title: Two Moves for the Bishop
steps.text:
White is not leaving a knight to be taken. {{Ng3}} pushes the bishop along, {{Bg6}} keeps the diagonal, and {{h4}} threatens to push again and drive the bishop off it for good. {{h6}} clears h7, so the bishop always has one square behind it.

Count what that cost. Black moved one bishop twice. White moved the knight again and sent a rook's pawn two squares out in front of the king.

Both sides spent time. Only one of them spent it on pawns, and a pawn does not come back.

steps.title: Paying Later Instead of Now
steps.text:
Black is behind in development here, and the Caro-Kann admits it. Three of Black's first four moves went on pawns, so White finishes first and gets to choose where the game is fought.

What the time bought is a structure White cannot bite into, a king that can go to either wing, and the bishop on g6 breathing free air outside its own pawns.

White's h-pawn, meanwhile, is never coming home. Pieces come off, the attack runs out, and that pawn is still standing where the king used to be safe.

steps.title: White Refuses the Trade
steps.text:
A different White, and only move three. Rather than trade in the middle, this one shoves the pawn past it and locks the door: a white pawn on e5, a white pawn on d4, and Black's pawn on d5 with nowhere to go.

Two pawns on a diagonal, the back one feeding the front one, are a **pawn chain**. White's runs d4 to e5. The pawn on e5 does the damage — it takes f6 away from Black's knight — and d4 is what holds it there. Nothing but pieces holds up d4.

So a chain is attacked at the foot, never at the head.

steps.title: Out First, Wall Second
steps.text:
Black's problem is the old problem. With the center locked, ...e6 has to come — it props up d5 and lets the kingside pieces breathe — and it is the same pawn that would shut the bishop in.

So the order does the work. {{Bf5}} goes first. White answers {{Nf3}}, and only then {{e6}}: the wall goes up behind the bishop instead of in front of it. {{Be2}}, and Black is ready.

> Get your worst piece out before you build the wall that would trap it.

steps.prompt: Attack the pawn holding White's chain up, using the only pawn of yours that can reach it.
steps.hint: Trace White's chain down to the pawn that no other pawn defends, then ask which of yours can get at it.
